title: Crown RC 5700 Entry-Bar Alarm and Slow Stop: Capture the Safety Response
summary: When an operator contacts the Entry Bar safety switch during travel on a Crown RC 5700 stand-up forklift, the alarm sounds and the truck slows to a stop. Here is what the official operator manual specifies and how to handle unexplained activation.
body_text: OSHA Compliance, Service Boundaries, and Dispatch Protocol When an Entry Bar alarm sounds or a slow stop occurs in the absence of foot contact, the truck is not working correctly. The Crown manual gives a clear instruction: 'Don't use the truck if it's not working correctly. Notify your supervisor.' Facility staff and operators must never bypass, wedge, shim, or open the entry bar assembly. Under federal regulation OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(p)(1), any powered industrial truck found to be defective or unsafe must be immediately taken out of service until restored to safe operating condition. Section 1910.178(q)(1) mandates that all repairs be performed exclusively by authorized personnel. Submitting a clear dispatch record with the truck model, serial number, hour meter reading, and detailed observation allows qualified service technicians to conduct proper diagnostic procedures.

title: Interview Red Flags: How to Spot a Bad Employer Before You Take the Job
summary: The interview runs both ways. Learn the process, room, and offer red flags that reveal a bad employer, the questions that surface them, and when to walk.
body_text: How do you spot a bad employer before you take the job? Watch how they treat you while they still want something from you. A hiring process that ghosts you between rounds, an interviewer who never opened your resume, a recruiter who dodges "why is this role open?", or an offer you have to sign by tomorrow are all telling you something. One rough moment is a question. Three is an answer. The interview runs both ways, so screen them as hard as they screen you, and weigh what you find against how much you need the paycheck. Most job-search advice treats the interview like a test you pass or fail. It is not. It is a first date where both people are deciding whether to see each other again, except one of you is pretending it is only a test. The company spends the hour probing you for reasons to say no. You are allowed to do the exact same thing. The trouble is that wanting a job badly makes you generous. You explain away the recruiter who called you the wrong name. You tell yourself the three-week silence between rounds was "just how busy they are." You accept the offer that came with a forty-eight-hour fuse because saying no feels reckless when rent is due. Then you start, and week two confirms every signal you talked yourself out of. This is a guide to reading those signals in real time, from the candidate's side of the table. Not to make you paranoid. Plenty of what looks like a red flag is just a small company running lean, or one overloaded scheduler having a bad week. The skill is telling the difference between a quirk you can live with and a pattern that tells you how you will be treated once they no longer need to impress you. The interview is a two-way evaluation, and desperation makes you forget it Here is a thing recruiters say out loud that job seekers rarely think about: they are reading you constantly. The rambling answer, the candidate who did zero research, the person who only asks about pay, the one who trashes every past employer. Recruiters keep running lists of these. If the room is that full of signal for them, it is exactly that full of signal for you. The people interviewing you cannot help revealing what the place is actually like. Desperation is what turns that off. When you have been searching for four months, or you got laid off two weeks into the hunt, your threshold for "acceptable" quietly drops until almost nothing registers as a warning. That is human. It is also the exact mechanism that lands people in jobs they quit within a quarter. The cost of a missed red flag is not embarrassment. It is six months of your life, a gap you now have to explain, and a re-entry into the same brutal search you were trying to escape. So the honest version of this advice is not "walk out at the first sign of trouble." It is: notice the signal, do not delete it just because you need the money, and then make a clear-eyed call with your actual options in view. A person sitting on two other offers gets to be picky. A person with three weeks of runway is playing a different game and should know it. The flags do not change. What changes is what you can afford to do about them. Red flags in the process, before you even meet anyone A company's hiring process is the one part of its operation you get to see for free. If it is a mess, that is not a fluke you are catching them on. It is a preview. Chaos and getting your name wrong. Reschedules that pile up, interviews confirmed then quietly cancelled, an email that opens with someone else's name. A single slip is nothing; everyone fat-fingers a calendar. But when a company cannot keep its own candidates straight and then doubles down instead of a quick "sorry, my mistake," you have learned two things at once. They are disorganized, and they are bad at owning it. Both of those follow you into the job. Ghosting between rounds. You do three interviews, they promise "next steps by Friday," and then nothing for three weeks. Sometimes you find out the role is dead only because the reposted listing shows up in your feed. A hiring team that treats a finalist this way while it is trying to woo them is showing you its default setting. Respect during the chase is the ceiling, not the floor. It only goes down from here. The rounds that never end. Four, six, eight stages for a role that is not running a nuclear reactor. Some of that is a genuinely thorough process. A lot of it is indecision, a hiring manager who will not commit, or a team using free candidate time to think out loud. If the loop keeps expanding with no clear finish line, that is worth weighing carefully, and we wrote a whole survival guide on why interview loops have ballooned and when to walk . The huge unpaid take-home. A short skills check is fair. A twenty-hour "project" that looks suspiciously like a real deliverable is a different animal. Watch especially for the take-home that arrives after they have already dragged you through several rounds; that is often less about assessing you and more about keeping your hope alive. As general guidance, US wage law turns on whether you are doing real, productive work: a brief simulated exercise or a short skills test is usually fine to leave unpaid, but if you are producing work the company can actually use, that starts to look like labor they should be paying for.If a stranger asks you to do their actual work for free before they have committed to anything, it is fair to ask what they would be like as a boss. An all-automated pipeline with no human in it. A recorded one-way video screen answered into a camera, an AI scoring pass, and still no live person by the third stage. The format itself is not proof of a bad employer; overloaded teams use it as a first-pass filter. But a pipeline engineered so that nobody has to actually talk to you until very late tells you where you rank in their attention. We broke down how one-way and AI video interviews actually work , and separately, whether refusing one is worth the cost . Hiding the pay. A company that will not name a range, keeps deflecting the salary question, and clearly wants to "sell" you on the mission before it drops a number is usually protecting a number worth hiding. The version of this that should end the conversation is the one where they lowball hard on a call after all that buildup, treating the whole courtship as a closing technique. Churn urgency and the role that keeps reopening "We need someone who can start yesterday." Said once about a genuine backfill, that is just honesty. Said with a certain frantic edge, repeated across the whole process, it points at churn: people keep leaving, the team keeps scrambling, and you are the next warm body they hope will stop the bleeding. Urgency that feels like a fire drill is rarely about you being special. It is about a hole they cannot keep filled. A close cousin is the role that keeps reappearing. If you notice the same job reposted every few months, or the interviewer lets slip that the last two people "didn't work out," pay attention. Sometimes a role is genuinely growing and they need three of you. Often it is a seat nobody stays in, and the reason nobody stays is the thing they are not telling you. The tell you can catch live is how they answer when you ask why it is open. Which brings us to the questions that do the real work. Red flags in the interview itself The process shows you the machine. The interview shows you the people. This is where a bad employer leaks the most, because a human being under mild social pressure struggles to hide contempt, chaos, or fear. The interviewer who never read your resume. They ask you to "walk them through your background" not as an opener but because they genuinely do not know it. They mix you up with another candidate. They arrive fifteen minutes late with no apology, or an hour late while you sit there deciding whether to leave. None of this is a scheduling accident. It is a statement about how much your time is worth to them, delivered before you have signed anything. They dodge "why is this role open?" A confident, healthy team answers this easily: someone got promoted, we are growing, the last person moved to another department. A vague non-answer, a subject change, or visible discomfort is information. Recruiters themselves treat a candidate's vague, evasive answers as a red flag; the same rule applies when you point the question back at them. They badmouth the last person in the seat. If the hiring manager trashes your predecessor to you, a stranger, in an interview, sit with that for a second. That is who they will be about you the moment you leave. The same goes for casual contempt about current staff, other departments, or "people who just don't get it here." You are hearing the internal weather report. "We're a family." This one is worth naming precisely, because it sounds warm and functions as a trap. Family framing is the language companies reach for when they want loyalty they have not earned and boundaries they can quietly erase. The clearest tell shows up around time off: the outfit that calls itself a family and then treats an approved vacation as a betrayal, or reschedules your leave because they "can't function without you." The honest response to that is the one that cuts through it. If they cannot survive a week without you, that is a staffing failure, not a compliment, and it is certainly not a reason to skip your trip. Great teams describe how they work. Bad ones describe how much they will need from you. They cannot describe success. Ask what a strong first ninety days looks like, or how someone succeeds in this role, and a good manager has a real answer ready. A blank, a platitude, or "just, you know, hit the ground running" often means they have not thought about it, which means you will be steering in the dark with a boss who cannot tell you where the shore is. Hostile tactics, invasive questions, and the room itself Some red flags are not about disorganization at all. They are about what the company thinks it is entitled to ask of a stranger. Stress tactics and the "will you let us exploit you" test. Some interviews turn hostile on purpose: a deliberately rude interviewer, an aggressive line of questioning, a scenario built to rattle you. Occasionally that is a clumsy attempt to test composure. Often it is a preview of the management style. The sharpest version is the question dressed up as a screening item that is really asking whether you will let them take advantage of you, some flavor of "are you okay with long hours and no extra pay?" or "we ask a lot here, is that a problem?" A team that opens by probing your tolerance for being used is telling you what the job is. There are also the trap questions that feel unfair by design, and we covered how to read and answer the interview questions built to throw you so you can tell a real test from a warning. Invasive, off-limits questions. Being asked what your parents do for a living, whether your father is fine with you working, whether you have kids or plan to, your age, where you are "really" from. In the US several of these touch legally protected categories, so an interviewer wandering into them is either careless or does not care, and both are a culture signal. General guidance, not legal advice, but the instinct is right: questions with no bearing on whether you can do the job are usually a probe for something they should not be weighing, and a window into how the place thinks. The people who already work there. If you get an office visit or a tour, look up. Staff who will not make eye contact, who go quiet when the manager walks by, who look like they are counting down, are giving you an unfiltered read no scripted answer can match. A useful move is to ask where you would actually be sitting and have them show you. It forces concreteness, and it puts you in the room with the people whose faces you are trying to read. Red flags in the offer You made it to yes. This is the stage where a bad employer, sensing the finish line, stops performing. Do not relax yet. They will not put it in writing. Comp, title, start date, bonus structure, equity, all of it belongs in a document you can read twice. A company that keeps the terms verbal, gets cagey when you ask for a written offer, or "clarifies" the number downward after the handshake is showing you how it handles commitments. Everything you agree to on a call and cannot point to later is something you may have to fight for on your worst day. Vagueness about the actual role. If you are three interviews deep and still cannot get a straight description of what you would do all day, who you report to, or how the job is measured, that is not a detail they forgot. Ambiguity at the offer stage often means the role itself is undefined, which means your first year will be a slow argument about what your job even is. The exploding offer. A short, high-pressure deadline, sign in twenty-four or forty-eight hours or the offer disappears, is one of the most reliable signals of a company negotiating from insecurity. It is widely recognized as a desperate-employer move for a simple reason: an outfit confident in its offer does not need to detonate your ability to think it over. If they manufacture a crisis to get your signature now, they will manufacture crises weekly once you are inside. We wrote a calm script for handling a lowball or high-pressure offer without blowing it up , and a full framework for weighing one offer against another on more than base salary . The pulled offer after a polite counter. A single, reasonable, in-band counter almost never gets an offer yanked. When it does, that is not a negotiation, it is a personality reveal. An employer that gets offended by a normal ask, or quietly moves on to candidate number two the moment you push back gently, is telling you it will treat every future raise and promotion the same way. Good-faith negotiation is a two-way skill; the absence of it now predicts its absence forever. Want to walk in ready to read the room? Practice the questions that surface a bad employer, and your answers to their trickier ones, with Hiration's Interview Prep. Prep smarter → The questions that surface all of this You do not have to guess. A handful of plain, sincere questions pull most of these flags into the open, and they double as the strong closing questions that make you look serious rather than desperate. The trick is that you are watching the answer, not just whether they will answer. Why is this role open? Backfill, growth, and churn all sound different. Listen for whether the reason is specific and comfortable or vague and evasive. What happened to the person who had it? A promotion is a good sign. A quiet "they left" with no elaboration, or worse, a little dig at them, is worth a follow-up. This pairs naturally with asking about typical reasons people move on from the team . What does success look like in the first ninety days? This forces the manager to reveal whether they have actually thought about the role. A crisp answer is reassuring, while a fumble tells you that you would be steering without a map. How would you describe the team's typical hours? Asked plainly, it is hard to dodge without the dodge itself being an answer. "It depends on the season" is normal. A long pause followed by "we're pretty flexible, we all just care a lot" is the sound of unpaid overtime being rebranded. What has turnover been like on this team over the last year or two? Some interviewers will give you a real number. Some will get uncomfortable. Both responses tell you something. Where would I actually be sitting? Concrete, disarming, and it puts you physically among the people you are trying to read. For more on framing these, our guide to the questions worth asking your interviewer goes deeper on tone and timing. One caution, because recruiters see through hollow versions of these. A question like "is there anything on my resume you're worried about?" reads as a gotcha and rarely lands. Ask because you genuinely want to know how the place runs, not to score a point. And remember that the point of asking is to watch the reaction. A company that squirms at "why is this role open?" has answered you whether or not it says a word. How to weigh a red flag against your leverage This is the part most red-flag listicles skip, and it is the part that matters. A flag is not a verdict. It is a data point you weigh against three things: your leverage, the market you are actually in, and the specific situation you are in right now. Start by separating quirks from patterns. A founder running a scrappy, slightly chaotic process at a five-person startup earns a lot more slack than a hundred-person company that ghosts its finalists, and one awkward interviewer weighs almost nothing next to a whole room of people who avoid your eyes. Small companies genuinely are messier. A young team without a polished machine will fumble things a mature one would not, and some of what reads as a flag is just that texture. Do not pathologize normal. Then be honest about a couple of things people routinely misread. Expecting occasional extra hours from a salaried, exempt role is legal and common; demanding unpaid overtime from an hourly worker is not, and a company that blurs that line on day one is worth watching. Being straight with you about a rough job market is fine, even helpful. The problem starts when a recruiter uses that market as cover for treating you badly. The signal is rarely the fact itself; it is the attitude wrapped around it. Now weigh it. One yellow flag is a question you carry into the next conversation. A cluster of them, the disorganized process and the evasive answers and the exploding offer, is your answer. And the size of the flag you can accept scales with your options. If you have runway and other irons in the fire, hold your standards high; a place that fumbles the courtship rarely improves after you sign. If you are running out of money, you may take the imperfect job with your eyes open, keep your résumé warm, and treat it as a bridge rather than a destination. That is a legitimate strategy, not a failure. Taking a flawed job on purpose is not the mistake here; walking in blind to flaws you could have spotted is. When to walk, and what to do afterward If your gut is screaming and you can afford to listen, listen. The interviews people remember most fondly years later are often the ones they walked away from. Walking does not have to be dramatic. You can finish the conversation politely, thank them, and simply not move forward, or pull your application with a short, civil note. You owe a company that showed you its worst nothing more than that. And if you have already taken the job and the flags have turned real, that is a different problem with a different playbook, which we cover in our guide to recognizing and handling a toxic workplace once you are inside one . For the bigger picture on how the whole pipeline works from application to offer, our walkthrough of how hiring actually works puts each of these moments in context. You are not being difficult by evaluating them. You are doing the same job they are doing to you, just with less power and higher stakes, which is exactly why you cannot afford to skip it. Frequently Asked Questions What are the biggest interview red flags for a bad employer? A few show up again and again: a disorganized process that ghosts you between rounds, an interviewer who clearly never read your resume, evasive answers to "why is this role open?", casual badmouthing of the last person in the seat, "we're a family" used to justify no boundaries, and an offer with a same-day deadline. Any one of these might have an innocent explanation. Two or three together rarely do. Is it okay to interview the employer back? It is more than okay, it is necessary. The interview is a mutual evaluation, and the company is already reading you closely the whole time. Asking sharp, sincere questions about the role, the team, and why the seat is open makes you look serious, not entitled. The worst outcome is that a genuinely good employer respects you more for it. Why is "why is this role open?" such a useful question? Because the answer separates growth from churn, and because the way they answer matters as much as the words. "We're expanding" or "she got promoted" is a good sign. A vague deflection, visible discomfort, or a dig at your predecessor tells you the seat may be one nobody stays in, and that the reason is something they would rather not say out loud. Is a long unpaid take-home assignment a red flag? It depends on the size and the timing. A short skills check is normal. A sprawling project that looks like real, usable work is not, especially if it lands after several rounds, which often means they are dragging out your hope. As general guidance, US wage law turns on whether you are doing real, productive work the company can use; if you are, that starts to resemble labor they should pay for, while a purely simulated skills test usually is not. This is not legal advice, just a good instinct to trust. What does "we're a family" really mean at a company? Sometimes it is harmless enthusiasm. Often it is code for loyalty they have not earned and boundaries they intend to erase. The tell is what happens around time off and after-hours asks. A place that calls itself a family and then treats your approved vacation as a betrayal has shown you the real deal. Healthy teams describe how they work, not how much they will need from you. Is an exploding offer with a 24-hour deadline a bad sign? Usually, yes. A company confident in its offer does not need to detonate your ability to think it over. High-pressure "decide now" deadlines are a well-known signal of an employer negotiating from insecurity, and the pressure rarely stops after you sign. Asking politely for a few days is reasonable, and how they react to that request is itself a test worth running. Can an employer legally ask about my family, parents, or age? In the US, several of these areas touch legally protected categories, so a question about your age, kids, marital status, or where you are "really" from is at minimum careless and often a culture warning. General information, not legal advice: questions with no bearing on whether you can do the job are usually a probe for something an interviewer should not be weighing, and a window into how the place thinks. How do I tell a real red flag from a small-company quirk? Separate quirks from patterns. A lean startup with a slightly chaotic scheduler is not the same as a big company that ghosts finalists. Expecting occasional extra hours from a salaried role is normal; demanding unpaid overtime from an hourly worker is not. The signal is rarely the fact itself, it is the attitude wrapped around it, and whether the flags cluster. Should I take a job with red flags if I really need the money? Sometimes, with your eyes open. A flag is a data point you weigh against your leverage. If you have runway and other options, hold your standards high. If money is tight, you can take an imperfect job as a bridge, keep your resume warm, and plan to move on. That is a strategy, not a failure. The only real mistake is not seeing the flaws before you sign. What if I only realize the employer is bad after I start? That is a different situation with its own playbook. Once you are inside, the questions become how to protect yourself, whether to stay while you search, and when it is time to leave. title: Vision Over Hype: How Ethan Glenn Built Every Other Thursday Without Chasing Algorithms
summary: How Ethan Glenn turned 20 custom hats into Every Other Thursday, a multimillion-dollar bootstrapped apparel empire.
body_text: Ethan Glenn never planned to start a clothing brand. Every Other Thursday began as a mood board on Instagram: vintage cars, old catalogs, the drape of a well-worn jacket. But one day he made a single hat with the account’s name on it and wore it in his videos—and people started asking to buy it. That one hat grew into a multimillion-dollar apparel brand with a retail store in New York City, built with no outside investment and no formal fashion training. Drawing on a background in photography and marketing, Glenn grew the company one drop at a time, reading demand signal by signal. Here’s how he converted an audience into a business, funded every step from cash flow, kept his own face off the brand on purpose, and stayed disciplined about what he makes. On making one hat and discovering a business by accident: I actually had no desire to start a clothing brand. That was never on my vision board or anything I’d looked toward. I came from a marketing background—a lot of photography and video—but I had a bit of a personal brand and this mood board on Instagram where I posted cool photos. One summer I just made a hat with the name “Every Other Thursday” on it, which was the mood board’s name at the time. I was wearing it in my videos, and people were like, “Oh, can I buy that hat?” And I was like, “I guess.” So I made 20 hats, and they sold out in a couple minutes. That’s when I thought, “Wait a second, what else could I make?” It just kind of snowballed, and within 12 to 18 months it was a full-fledged merch brand. It was evolving faster than I could keep up with. When you see a demand for something, you kind of have to jump on it—so that’s what I did. On the “look around my apartment” method for deciding what to make next: Hats were just what I was wearing a lot of at the time. I still am—I’m wearing one right now. And it’s an easy first purchase for a customer. It’s relatively cheap compared to everything else. So after the hat did well, I looked around my apartment and asked, “What can I turn into a product and use in my content?” I had this cool loft apartment that was a big part of my content, and I was always taking photos of the interior—the coffee table, whatever it was. So I made a little ashtray with the logo on it. I could set it on a pile of books, shoot my living room, and tag it. That worked. Then I looked around again and thought, “I use a wallet every day, so why don’t I make a leather wallet?” I kept building with small pieces that were realistically easy enough to make my own—no full cut-and-sew garment, nothing too difficult. I just kept looking at my daily-use items and asking what I could turn into a product. Every Other Thursday is dedicated to creating a classic and timeless look. Every Other Thursday On treating his audience as a finite resource worth converting fast: Before I had an audience of my own, I worked for a couple of influencers in the million-follower realm in Toronto—doing their photo, their video, their editing. So I saw the power of a large audience early. Part of that is brand deals, but part of it is the ability to channel an audience into a company and have this built-in ready-to-purchase customer base. When I started growing my own following, I thought, “I don’t want to be an influencer forever. That’s not something I see doing for decades. So what can I do to capitalize on this momentum right now?” Because for a lot of people, it doesn’t last forever. In my mind, an audience is a finite resource, whereas the brand could just infinitely grow into a much larger being regardless of audience size. That’s the difference. You don’t see an influencer carrying the same weight as a legacy company. So when the hat took off, our motto became: If it’s working, let’s just go as fast as possible. I put all my eggs in that basket, hired a production manager in LA, and started fueling the beast. On funding every drop with the last one instead of taking investment: Ever since the beginning, it’s just funded itself. I never put money in, and we’ve never taken investment. The first 20 hats sold, and I took that money and paid for the next 80. That sold, and I paid for the ashtrays. It snowballed from there, and every drop was bigger than the last. For the first year and a half or two years, it was very drop-based. The website would sit empty for months at a time with nothing to shop, because we’d taken all our available capital and put it into the next batch. That was the whole model. Coming from a marketing background helped a lot, because one of the most expensive parts of building a brand is the marketing side—photo shoots, editing, emails, the website. That was all stuff I already knew how to do, so I didn’t have to pay for any of it. Every dollar we made for the first few years went straight into making more product. And for the first two or three years, I don’t think we ran a single ad. My personal audience was still converting on its own. Ethan took his brand beyond the online market and created a brick-and-mortar store in New York City. Every Other Thursday On why he kept his face off the brand from day one: We always kept the two separate. If you followed me, you got the behind-the-scenes—the sampling, the building of a brand, all the stuff that’s interesting to watch. But if you followed Every Other Thursday, you only saw the brand. You didn’t see my face. It was its own beast. We always hired models. I was never the model, so it could grow on its own. A lot of people fall into the trap where the only way they’ll sell a product is if their face and name is attached to it. You see it with influencer-led brands—you follow the person, they make the product, and because they’re selling it, you want it. But if that person disappeared one day and it was only the company left, maybe you’re not as interested anymore. Because I built the two as independent verticals, the brand got its own legs a lot quicker. It’s funny—about six months ago we opened a store here in New York, and I’ll be in the shop helping out, and someone will come in and go, “Sorry, do you work here?” We get to talking and they ask, “How long have you worked here?” And I say, “Well, it’s actually my business.” That’s the payoff. I look at the J.Crews of the world—they’ve been around for decades, and there’s a reason their name carries weight. On “building sideways” instead of into a million categories: I’m not a very big fashion person. I’m just making the things I actually wear every day. We only have one pair of jeans right now, because those are the only ones the team wants. Having that specific viewpoint has really sharpened our product catalog. People ask how you get repeat customers off a narrow catalog, and for us it’s about building sideways rather than building into a million different categories. Our bestselling pants are our fatigue pants—a classic military cut, and our most popular color is this beautiful faded green that looks like old army pants. We spent a lot of time getting the fabric and fit right. People buy it, love how it fits, then come back for a different color. This year we introduced a linen version—in theory the exact same pant, but it feels and looks completely different because the fabric is so different. Then you build out the wardrobe. You start with the pants, then the shirt—but there are 10 different options in a shirt, whether it’s color, fabric, pattern, or print. Same general fit, but a blank white cotton and a plaid linen are vastly different. That’s how you end up with customers who have 10, 20, 30 orders under their belt. It starts with one, they like how it fits, and it multiplies from there. The basics earn the trust. Once a customer knows the shirt fits great, they’re more inclined to take a chance on something a little more out there. The trap I’ve fallen into before is thinking, “I need to make that because it’s what’s cool right now.” I’ve really focused on not doing that. Having a specific idea of what your world and vision look like matters more than chasing a trend. Every Other Thursday is designed to appeal to men interested in a classic Americana feel. Every Other Thursday On learning he can’t do everything: I’m a workaholic. I could do everything all day long, and part of me wants to. But that’s not good for me, and it’s not good for the company, because true growth comes from having other ideas in the room—people who are better suited for different skill sets than I am. So over the past year and a half, we’ve hired across the board: retail employees, people on the brand side. That’s opened up my creative ideas, because I’m not bogged down in production schedules or dealing with the warehouse day to day. At some point you hit a burnout stage where you’re too tired or too mentally exhausted to make anything. I’m the creative fuel of the company, and your growth stops if you can’t keep being creative and interesting. So the biggest thing I’ve learned is that I don’t need to do everything. Building the team on the back end is what lets me keep doing the part only I can do. Hear Ethan’s full conversation on Shopify Masters for more on how skipping wholesale keeps his prices under market, why he doesn’t love TikTok, even though it’s where he blew up, and how each city he’s lived in quietly decided the company’s next move.

title: Chevron Announces Leadership Changes
summary: • Navin Mahajan to retire after nearly 30 years with the company • Uriel "Ose” Oseguera named Treasurer of Chevron HOUSTON --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 12, 2026-- Chevron Corporation (NYSE: CVX) today announced the election of Uriel "Ose" Oseguera as Treasurer, effective November 1, 2026.
body_text: Press Release < Back View Printer friendly Version 08/12/26 Chevron Announces Leadership Changes • Navin Mahajan to retire after nearly 30 years with the company • Uriel "Ose” Oseguera named Treasurer of Chevron HOUSTON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 12, 2026-- Chevron Corporation (NYSE: CVX) today announced the election of Uriel "Ose" Oseguera as Treasurer, effective November 1, 2026. Oseguera succeeds Navin Mahajan, who will retire from Chevron after nearly 30 years of service. As Treasurer, Oseguera will lead Chevron's treasury organization, including capital markets, corporate finance, insurance, credit and risk management activities. He will report to Chevron Chief Financial Officer Eimear Bonner. Oseguera currently serves as Vice President, Upstream Business Performance & Finance. “Ose brings an exceptional combination of treasury expertise, global business leadership, and deep company knowledge to the Treasurer role," said Bonner. “His experience across corporate finance, capital markets, and international business leadership provides a distinctive perspective on risk management, financial discipline, and value creation. Coupled with strong relationships across the enterprise and sound judgment, Ose is exceptionally well positioned to advance Chevron's strong financial position and long-term value.” Oseguera joined Chevron in 1990. Over the course of his career, he has held leadership positions in finance, treasury and planning across Venezuela, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, and the United States. Prior to his current role, he served as General Manager of Chevron's Financial Shared Services organization. Oseguera earned a bachelor's degree in business administration from California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, and an MBA from Saint Mary's College of California. Mahajan has served as Chevron's Treasurer since 2019. During his career, he held leadership roles across treasury, finance, compliance, and business organizations globally. "Throughout his nearly 30 years with Chevron, Navin has been a trusted leader whose expertise, integrity, and commitment have strengthened our company and Finance organization," Bonner said. "You could always count on Navin when the challenges were most complex and the stakes were highest. His rare combination of innovation, discipline, and thoughtful decision-making enabled him to navigate complexity, inspire teams and deliver lasting impact." About Chevron Chevron is one of the world’s leading integrated energy companies. We believe affordable, reliable and ever-cleaner energy is essential to enabling human progress. title: For Summertime Cruising, Few Cars Top My ’73 Riviera
summary: This 1973 Buick Riviera GS is the beautiful queen of my driveway. My dad owned it before me, but before that, all I know of its history comes from a faded pink bill of sale I found in the glovebox. It is from Ken Logan Buick of Iowa and dated 9/11/73, and it appears to […]
body_text: This 1973 Buick Riviera GS is the beautiful queen of my driveway. My dad owned it before me, but before that, all I know of its history comes from a faded pink bill of sale I found in the glovebox. It is from Ken Logan Buick of Iowa and dated 9/11/73, and it appears to be a sales invoice for two vehicles totaling $8,148.65. My dad doesn’t remember a lot of purchase-day details, but his story of acquiring the Riv in the late ’80s or early ’90s has one fun anecdote: He said he was driving it back home to Rockford, Illinois, with my younger brothers following him across Iowa, and that my brothers had trouble keeping up in their ’88 Mustang GT. I guess he had to “see what she can do” or “blow out the carbon” on the highway across those endless cornfields. Ken Maupin Shortly after he got it, Dad had the factory vinyl top removed when he had the Riv repainted in its current white, which is just a bit whiter than the ivory coat it wore originally. Considering she has no clearcoat, the car still shines up nicely with hand-applied Meguiar’s carnuba. Dad owned a series of 10 Rivieras throughout my childhood—at least a few at a time, and a few of every year from ’66 through ’70 (plus this ’73 ). He would acquire them rather impulsively and store them about town in rented parking spaces under apartment buildings and such, often without Mom knowing about them. He’d have the insurance and registration paperwork mailed to his dry-cleaning business, where he could catch them. One day, though, he made the mistake of using the home address on one of them and Mom saw it at home. She warned him that he’d better come clean with all of them right then and there, since we’d never know where they were if he died (there may have been another thinly veiled threat in there as well). Ken Maupin Overall, Mom was a pretty good sport about his car problem, and we all believe she liked to be seen in nice cars, though she’d refuse to admit it at the risk of being his “enabler.” As I write this, it occurs to me that he probably used this very situation to get her to go along with making their home’s 2.5-car garage into a “7.5-car” garage by knocking the back down and building it way, way out. My job, prior to getting my driver’s license, was to start the Rivs periodically and keep them washed and waxed, and I only fell more in love with them by touching their curves and polishing their chrome. This ’73 Riviera GS then ended up being the last Rivera he owned. In the 2010s, as he neared retirement and had sold off various cars to help his kids with college or their life-needs, he ended up with only this one. It was the remaining token of his booming Riviera years, and so it was extra special to me, too. I had told him once that if he decided to sell this last one, I wanted dibs. Of course, when that day came, it was a bad time for me, right in the middle of helping my own kids through college, but we cut a payment deal, and he signed over the title trusting I wouldn’t skip town with it before payoff… Ken Maupin Ken Maupin A Google search says they only made 3933 GS models in 1973, out of 34,080 Rivieras that year. I’m not sure how many of those 3933 got the center console and the power factory sunroof (installed by American Sunroof Co., subsidiary of GM), but I think those surely add to this car’s intrinsic worth and sheer desirability for cruising. To me, the big, striking body outside says luxury coupe while the console shift and 455 V-8 say youthful power, so it’s like I’m driving luxury muscle. Dad had driven the car very little in the years before I got it, so it had needs before it could be a safe sunny-weekend cruiser . I started by getting the odo and fuel gauge fixed, so that I could at least tell when the 455 had drunk all of the 93 non-ethanol. I was thrilled to learn that even back in ’73, luxury features included a low fuel light. It goes on and off a lot as fuel sloshes in the tank when you near empty. Dad and I love cars, but we aren’t mechanics, so we have to locate those rare trustworthy local shops or guys somebody knows who are reasonably priced and do good work. Fortunately, I have been blessed with a dear, gifted friend who is happy for the hangout time while he does the actual fixing, and I just buy the replacement thing and then hand down wrenches or hold the flashlight. We are, however, the kind of enthusiasts who like to drive our cars. We keep them running, keep them washed and waxed, and grace the townspeople with them on errand day, when we catch breakfast with some pals, or when driving the missus to an early dinner. Ken Maupin So, she’s a survivor. Other than Dad nixing the vinyl roof and repainting, I added Pertronix ignition and Flowmaster Delta 50 mufflers on stainless steel dual pipes with chrome outlets, since the originals were rotted out. This makes the Riv more cruise-able, and it just sounds great, of course. But each season there is something to repair or replace. The huge doors had chewed half-way through those big pins in the back of the door jamb, so they needed shimming and new door handles. But, hey, the vacuum-operated cruise control works (even the dash indicator), as does the vacuum-operated trunk release in the glove box. The AM/FM radio works—not that I listen to it instead of the Flowmasters—and so does the fan under the huge rear window tray to keep the glass clear. Dad doesn’t know when the A/C stopped working or when the power sunroof came off the chain—a very expensive fix—but it manually slides open and closed, so since I only drive in the sun, I just slide it back with my hands and go. Midsummer cruises are pretty warm when you aren’t moving—that 455 makes a few BTUs—but most of the time, with the long door windows down, no mid-pillars, and the roof open, the “5-window A/C” is fine for cruising. It’s also an optimal configuration to acknowledge the honks, thumbs-up, and hollers of appreciation for the rolling artwork she is in this world of transportation blobs. Ken Maupin A few years ago, we went through a minor identity crisis when I installed BFG Radial T/As in place of the old white walls. She looked more sporty, but my own gut told me that the factory rally wheels, GS letters, console, and the 455 say just enough, and that the T/As were… yelling. Now back on whitewalls, we are all quite content. If my ship comes in some day, I’ll attend to the sunroof, A/C, and some other minor issues, get a $10K paintjob, and have the rally wheels re-chromed. But any work would have to take place in the winter, because I can’t give up any of those precious three-season driving days in my beautiful Riv. title: GoofyFS vs s3fs?
summary: Compares s3fs and Goofys, two tools for mounting S3 as a local filesystem, and explains how their metadata handling, caching strategies, and API usage impact performance, consistency, and cost. Helps teams understand when filesystem-on-S3 layers are sufficient—and when object-native approaches are a better fit for large-scale data workloads.
body_text: Introduction You’re a data engineer facing a familiar problem: Amazon S3 is powerful, scalable, and durable, but the moment you try to use it like a traditional filesystem, friction appears. Operations that are trivial on disk expand into high-latency API calls, unexpected performance cliffs, and costs driven by metadata rather than data. The question isn’t whether S3 works, but how far you can safely push it behind filesystem semantics. To close that gap, teams often reach for filesystem-on-S3 tools. Two of the most common options are s3fs and GOOFYfs . Both allow you to mount an S3 bucket as part of a local directory tree, but they make very different design tradeoffs in how they translate POSIX filesystem operations onto object storage—tradeoffs that matter more as data size, file counts, and concurrency increase. This article breaks down those tradeoffs. We’ll explain why making S3 behave like a filesystem is inherently hard, compare how s3fs and GOOFYfs handle that mismatch, and then step back to examine when filesystem abstractions stop being the right tool altogether. For teams building or scaling data pipelines, we’ll also look at why application-level systems like Archil can offer a cleaner, more predictable alternative. Filesystem Approach s3fs and GOOFYfs are both filesystems that allow you to mount an S3 bucket and interact with it as though it were part of your local file hierarchy. Once mounted, applications can read files via open() , list directories via readdir() , and write data via write() just as they would on a local disk. Under the hood, these filesystems translate POSIX-style operations into S3 API requests. A directory listing becomes a prefix-based LIST call. A file write becomes a PUT of an object. A rename often becomes a copy followed by a delete. Each filesystem makes its own choices about caching, metadata handling, and request batching in an effort to mask the latency and semantics of object storage. This translation layer is where s3fs and GOOFYfs begin to diverge. Although they expose similar interfaces to applications, their internal strategies for managing metadata, consistency, and API pressure lead to very different performance and operational characteristics. Why Making S3 Behave Like a Filesystem Is Non-Trivial POSIX filesystems assume mutable files, fast metadata access, and synchronous visibility of changes. Object storage does not. S3 exposes immutable objects accessed through comparatively high-latency API calls and is optimized for throughput rather than per-operation responsiveness. As a result, even basic filesystem operations can expand into multiple S3 requests. A directory listing maps to a prefix scan. A rename operation requires a full object copy followed by a delete. Appends and partial writes often require rewriting the entire object. These costs compound quickly as file counts grow. The effectiveness of any filesystem-on-S3 solution is therefore dominated by how well it reduces, batches, or amortizes metadata operations. Design decisions around caching and request patterns matter more than raw storage bandwidth. s3fs: POSIX Fidelity Over Optimization s3fs prioritizes POSIX compatibility, translating filesystem calls into S3 operations in a relatively direct and transparent way. Metadata is frequently fetched from S3, and directory structure is inferred dynamically from object listings rather than maintained locally. This design minimizes abstraction complexity but makes s3fs highly sensitive to S3 latency and API overhead. Workloads involving recursive directory traversal, large numbers of small files, or concurrent opens can generate a large volume of LIST and HEAD requests. As datasets scale, performance degrades in proportion to object count rather than data volume. s3fs is therefore best suited to low-concurrency workloads where correctness and compatibility matter more than performance. GOOFYfs: Reducing API Pressure and Metadata Overhead GOOFYfs takes a more aggressive approach to minimizing S3 API interactions. Rather than resolving metadata on every operation, it caches directory state and file attributes locally, allowing repeated filesystem calls to complete without round-trips to S3. Reads and writes are chunked and parallelized, improving throughput for large objects. Directory listings benefit from cached results and fewer full prefix scans. By reducing the total number of S3 calls, GOOFYfs improves latency while also lowering operational costs. This comes with trade-offs. Aggressive caching can surface stale metadata in multi-writer environments, and local state may need to be rebuilt after node restarts. GOOFYfs accepts these compromises in favor of scalability and throughput. Real-World Behavior Recursive Directory Traversal Consider a bucket containing ~1 million small objects under date-based prefixes: find /mnt/s3/logs -type f | wc -l s3fs: Each traversal triggers repeated prefix LIST calls. Latency scales with object count, and the operation can take minutes. GOOFYfs: After the initial scan, cached directory state allows subsequent traversals to complete locally with minimal S3 interaction. This difference becomes critical in analytics workflows that repeatedly traverse the same directory trees. Rename and Checkpoint Writes A common pipeline pattern is writing temporary output and renaming it into place: mv output.tmp output.final On S3, this expands into: COPY s3://bucket/output.tmp → s3://bucket/output.final DELETE s3://bucket/output.tmp For large objects, this is an O(object size) operation. s3fs: Performs this synchronously and conservatively. GOOFYfs: Can pipeline or defer work, but still pays the full copy cost. This is a structural limitation of filesystem semantics on immutable object storage. Technical Comparison: s3fs vs GOOFYfs Metadata Management s3fs treats S3 as the source of truth, inferring directory structure dynamically and issuing frequent LIST and HEAD requests. This ensures consistency but produces high request volume. GOOFYfs amortizes metadata lookups via local caching, significantly reducing request pressure for metadata-heavy workloads. Read and Write Paths s3fs often rewrites entire objects for small changes and performs reads serially, making it sensitive to latency. GOOFYfs uses read-ahead, write buffering, and parallel transfers to better utilize network bandwidth, especially for large datasets. Concurrency and Consistency s3fs attempts to preserve POSIX semantics, which can lead to conservative locking and unpredictable behavior under concurrent writes. GOOFYfs relaxes some guarantees, designing around object storage behavior instead of emulating strict filesystem rules. Cost and Operational Impact High metadata request volume can make s3fs expensive at scale. GOOFYfs’ reduced API footprint lowers both latency and request-related costs in production environments. Beyond Filesystems: Archil’s Application-Level Approach Even with optimization, filesystem abstractions inherit a fundamental mismatch when placed on top of object storage. Every operation must be translated into filesystem semantics before being mapped to objects. Archil removes this layer entirely. It treats S3 as a store of immutable objects plus manifests rather than files and directories. A typical workflow: Writers upload immutable data objects. A small manifest object describes dataset versions. Readers consume data by reading the manifest, not scanning directories. This eliminates directory traversal, rename semantics, and inode emulation. Concurrency is handled explicitly via versioning rather than locks. When Each Approach Makes Sense Filesystem-based tools remain useful when legacy applications or existing workflows require POSIX semantics. Between the two, GOOFYfs offers a more scalable implementation for most production workloads. When building new systems or scaling data pipelines, application-level approaches like Archil avoid the filesystem mismatch altogether. Instead of working around object storage constraints, they align directly with them — resulting in more predictable performance and clearer failure modes.

title: PUCAI Score: Pediatric Ulcerative Colitis Activity Explained
summary: Understand the six PUCAI inputs, score bands, and role of separate labs.
body_text: The Pediatric Ulcerative Colitis Activity Index, or PUCAI, is a noninvasive clinical score for children and adolescents with UC . It uses six areas: abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, stool consistency, stool frequency, nighttime stools, and activity level. It does not require endoscopy and does not include CRP, ESR, hemoglobin, albumin, or fecal calprotectin. That design allows repeat assessment at home, clinic, or hospital, but it does not mean laboratory and endoscopic evidence are unimportant ( PUCAI appraisal ; pediatric IBD score review ). How the six PUCAI components work Abdominal pain is graded from none to pain that cannot be ignored. Rectal bleeding reflects the amount and proportion of stools containing blood. Stool consistency distinguishes formed from partially formed or completely unformed stools. Frequency is counted over 24 hours. Nocturnal activity asks whether bowel movements wake the child, while activity level records limitation of normal daily activity. The weighted components create a 0-to-85 total. Common bands are below 10 for remission, 10 to 34 for mild activity, 35 to 64 for moderate activity, and 65 or more for severe activity. Validation work supports 10 as a useful remission cutoff, but clinical decisions consider the child’s trajectory and complete assessment ( PUCAI appraisal ). Use consistent definitions and a full 24-hour observation when possible. Bowel preparation, infection, laxatives, menstrual symptoms, or a day with unusually restricted eating can change answers. A caregiver and young person may perceive pain or activity limitation differently, so recording both perspectives can help. Why there are no lab points PUCAI was built to measure pediatric UC activity without invasive testing. CRP and ESR reflect systemic inflammation; hemoglobin can show anemia; albumin may fall with inflammation, poor intake, or intestinal protein loss; fecal calprotectin reflects intestinal neutrophilic inflammation. None is part of the arithmetic. A normal CRP therefore does not lower PUCAI, and a high calprotectin does not raise it. These separate layers can disagree. Symptoms may improve before inflammation fully resolves, or frequent stools can persist for reasons other than active mucosal disease. Pediatric teams use PUCAI alongside laboratory trends, growth, stool testing when infection is possible, and endoscopic assessment when clinically indicated ( pediatric IBD score review ; STRIDE-II ). Why a high or rising PUCAI matters In hospitalized acute severe pediatric UC , repeated PUCAI measurements can help teams assess early treatment response and whether rescue therapy or surgery consultation should be considered. Studies have also examined the practicality of serial scoring in real-world pediatric care ( PUCAI feasibility study ). The score supports, rather than replaces, vital signs, examination, labs, imaging, and specialist judgment. Keep each component, not just the total, with the date and medication timing. Add stool frequency and blood, nighttime waking, activity, hydration, weight, temperature, CBC, CRP, ESR, albumin, electrolytes, calprotectin, and infection-test results. Contact the pediatric GI team urgently for rapid worsening, frequent bloody stools, severe pain or swelling, repeated vomiting, fever, fainting, marked sleepiness, or dehydration. PUCAI is powerful because it turns observable experiences into a repeatable trend. It is safest when caregivers use that trend to communicate promptly, not to adjust medicines independently. Questions that make the number more useful Before comparing this result with an older one, confirm that both records used the same named instrument, version, scoring range, and assessment window. Ask whether the total represents the worst segment, a sum across segments, an average, or a single day. If a clinician or study used a modified version, record exactly what was removed or added. Also check whether treatment, bowel preparation, infection, missed diary entries, or incomplete examination affected the inputs. A small apparent change may reflect measurement conditions rather than a meaningful change in disease. At a visit, useful questions include: What domain does this score measure? Which component drove the result? What would count as response or remission in this setting? Does the number need confirmation with blood work, stool testing, endoscopy, biopsy, or imaging? Is the goal to follow symptoms, current inflammation, structural damage, treatment response, or quality of life ? Asking these questions turns an unfamiliar total into a specific clinical conversation. For personal tracking, avoid combining unlike scores on one graph. Keep each instrument in its own series and place objective tests on parallel timelines. Save the source report because the component details may matter later. Note both the sample or procedure date and the date you received the result. Trends are easiest to interpret when the method and timing stay consistent. If the number conflicts with how you feel or with another test, bring the disagreement to your care team instead of choosing the result that seems most reassuring. body_text: Most healthcare organizations have a language access policy on paper. The problem is what happens at 2 AM on a Saturday when that policy can't get a certified interpreter to the bedside in time. The gap between policy and practice is where patient safety events actually occur. Below you'll find the scope of the problem, what the research says about harm, and what it takes to build a language access program that holds up when it counts, including the unscheduled encounters your policy was written for but may not actually cover. TLDR: 29.6 million people in the US have limited English proficiency; language gaps are a standing caseload reality, not an edge case In a review of 336 patient safety events, 82.4% involved an interpretation challenge, and a certified interpreter was absent in over half Section 1557 requires covered entities to provide language access at no cost; bilingual staff who self-identify as proficient do not meet the standard AI medical interpretation requires clinical-grade quality controls, including negation checks and dosage verification, not general-purpose translation tools Opalite Health provides real-time AI medical interpretation across 150+ languages, validated in a study with Johns Hopkins Medicine, and integrates with major EHRs What is a language barrier in healthcare? A patient describes chest pressure in Haitian Creole. The nurse hears something about the heart, nods, and moves on. Neither one is confused about tone or intent. They simply cannot exchange the words that matter. That gap is a language barrier. In a clinical setting, it happens when a patient and their care team do not share a common language or dialect, which limits their ability to trade clinically meaningful information like symptoms, medication instructions, and consent. It differs from ordinary communication difficulty. Two people who speak the same language can still talk past each other. A language barrier removes the shared vocabulary entirely, so the content of a medical conversation never lands, no matter the goodwill in the room. Language barrier in healthcare: scale and statistics For clinical leaders, the first question is usually about volume. Is this a handful of patients or a standing feature of the caseload? The numbers point to the latter. The United States is home to 29.6 million individuals with limited English proficiency in healthcare , a population facing persistent healthcare disparities despite legal protections meant to guarantee access, according to research on language access disparities . Coverage gaps compound the problem. People with limited English proficiency remain three times as likely to be uninsured as their English-proficient peers. A caseload of that size, with coverage gaps stacked on top, is a structural issue for any health system serving a diverse community. How language barriers affect patient safety When a patient cannot describe what hurts, the diagnosis starts blind. A missed allergy, a garbled dose, a symptom the clinician never hears because it never got translated. These are the failure points where language gaps harm LEP patients . The evidence is direct. A review of 336 patient safety events in Pennsylvania traced a striking share to communication breakdowns. In a review of 336 patient safety events, 82.4% involved an interpretation challenge, and more than half identified that a certified interpreter was not used because one was not available. Read that last part again. The interpreter existed as policy. It just was not there when the patient needed it. That absence is where the safety risk lives: delayed diagnoses, medication errors, incomplete histories, and consent signed without real understanding. Real-world examples of language barrier harm in clinical settings The abstractions get concrete fast once you sit in the room. Here are three failure patterns that show up repeatedly in documented safety events. The ad hoc interpreter and the wrong dose A daughter translates for her mother at discharge. The instruction is "once daily," but the family word she reaches for means "once per meal." Three doses go home instead of one. Medication errors cluster around untrained interpreters, because a well-meaning relative fills gaps with guesses. The symptom taken literally A patient says their stomach is "burning," a colloquial way of describing anxiety in some cultures. The clinician orders a GI workup and misses the panic disorder underneath. Idiom does not survive a literal handoff. The discharge plan nobody followed A wound-care regimen gets explained in English. The patient nods to be polite. Follow-up never happens. Readmission follows. The plan was sound, which is a reminder of why plain language in healthcare matters as much as translation. Cultural barriers and the health equity dimension Language is the wall you notice first. Culture is the one you walk into after you think the wall is gone. Even with a fluent interpreter present, a patient may describe pain through a framework the clinician does not recognize, a challenge taken on by cultural intelligence in medical interpretation , or defer to family before answering, or treat a consent form as a formality to sign instead of a decision to weigh. Health beliefs shape what a patient volunteers, withholds, and thinks a diagnosis means. Linguistic concordance, when a patient can speak in their own language, builds the trust that makes cultural gaps visible. Without it, patients often stay quiet. That silence tracks with worse outcomes . A patient who does not ask does not get corrected, and the misunderstanding rides home with them. For anyone accountable for equity, cultural and language barriers in healthcare rarely appear in isolation. Basic translation closes the language gap but often leaves the cultural one intact. A more durable approach pairs interpretation access with cultural humility training for bilingual staff and interpreters, so providers can recognize when a patient's framing reflects a cultural belief system instead of a clinical symptom. Capturing preferred language data in the EHR and tracking linguistic concordance rates as standing equity dashboard metrics lets health equity leaders measure the gap at the population level, where it actually lives. Research on language concordance and outcomes links matched-language encounters to higher preventive care uptake, better chronic disease control, and stronger patient retention, with improvements that appear in HEDIS scores and readmission data. Legal obligations: Section 1557 and language access requirements The safety risk is also a legal one. Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act, and its 2024 final rule, require covered entities to provide meaningful language access to patients with limited English proficiency at no charge. Covered entities means nearly every organization receiving federal funding, including Medicare and Medicaid participation. That is most of the industry. In December 2024, the HHS Office for Civil Rights issued a Dear Colleague letter restating these duties and clarifying standards for qualified interpreters and machine translation, per guidance on language accessibility expectations. Two lines matter for compliance leaders. You cannot make a patient supply or pay for their own interpreter. And leaning on bilingual staff who self-identify as proficient does not meet the standard under language access requirements . Strategies for overcoming language barriers in healthcare No single approach wins. Each modality trades availability against cost, speed, and accuracy, and gaps in access and outcomes for patients with limited English proficiency persist across all of them, per a systematic review of language access . (NYSE: STZ), a leading U.S.-based total beverage alcohol company, today announced an incremental $100 million investment over the next five years to support U.S. farmers in Idaho, Montana, and North Dakota, reinforcing the company’s long-term commitment to American agriculture and the vital role it plays in sustaining America’s iconic beer industry. The investment includes incremental purchases from American farmers and initiatives designed to help strengthen the future of these U.S. farming communities. This investment reflects the company’s continued commitment to U.S. farmers as they face sustained pressure from declining acreage, shifting demand, rising input costs, and weather-related challenges that have made it harder for many growers to maintain and expand their businesses. Barley, corn, and hops remain essential to the American beer industry and its extensive and multifaceted supply chain inclusive of U.S. farmers, maltsters, brewers, distributors, retailers, transportation and logistics partners, and local communities across the country. As part of this investment, Constellation Brands will partner with growers in Idaho, Montana, and North Dakota to identify opportunities that help sustain their farming operations for the long term. The company is establishing Constellation’s Farmers Future, a grower-led advisory committee that will bring together farmers, trade groups, and community leaders to help inform investments intended to strengthen agricultural resilience and the domestic agricultural supply chain. “U.S. barley, corn, and hops farmers are an essential part of the American economy and foundational to our business,” said Nicholas Fink, President and Chief Executive Officer of Constellation Brands. “Their work supports communities, drives economic activity across the supply chain, and makes it possible for our products to reach consumers across the country. We have deep respect for the persistence and expertise of these growers, especially after several challenging years for American farming, and we remain committed to continuing to support this foundational part of our supply chain.” Constellation Brands already invests more than $750 million annually with American farmers and suppliers, including purchasing approximately 80% of all U.S. barley exports. This commitment is part of the company’s broader economic impact in the U.S., where it invests more than $4.2 billion annually in employee wages, capital expenditures, and U.S. taxes. The company’s operations also support more than 100,000 American jobs across its supply chain. As part of this initiative, Constellation Brands will partner with growers and agricultural partners to determine how its investment can help support farm resiliency, market access, sustainability, and the continued economic vitality of farming communities in key producing states. "Idaho is proud to be one of the top barley-producing states in the nation, and this investment from Constellation Brands is great news for our farmers and rural communities. Our growers work hard every day to supply the barley that fuels a critical American industry. This kind of long-term partnership recognizes their contribution to Idaho and the U.S. economy,” said Idaho Governor Brad Little (R-ID). “North Dakota has a long and proud history as a barley-growing powerhouse, and we appreciate Constellation Brands investing in our farmers so they can continue to play a pivotal role in the U.S. beverage industry well into the future,” said North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong (R-ND). “Idaho is the nation’s leading producer of barley, and it is an important part of our state’s agricultural economy. An investment in Idaho barley is an investment in thousands of Idaho jobs and a commitment to American-grown crops. I commend this good news for Gem State growers,” said Idaho Senator Mike Crapo (R-ID). "Idaho's barley farmers are an important anchor in our agricultural economy and communities. This investment will support jobs and keep costs low for farmers across the Gem State as they help to feed the world,” said Idaho Senator Jim Risch (R-ID). "Montana's barley farmers are the backbone of our agricultural economy. This announcement comes at a critical time for our growers, and it shows what's possible when American companies invest in American farmers. I appreciate Constellation Brands' commitment to Montana and the Trump administration's continued focus on strengthening U.S. agriculture,” said Montana Governor Greg Gianforte (R-MT). "Ag is Montana’s top industry, and the hard work of our farmers and ranchers puts food on the table for millions of families across the country and around the world. The future of Montana relies heavily on our ag community, and investments like this will be critical to protect and promote Montana agriculture,” said Montana Senator Steve Daines (R-MT). “Montana’s farmers feed America, support good-paying jobs, and keep our rural communities strong. This investment is a major vote of confidence in Montana barley growers and will help family farms stay competitive and pass their operations on to the next generation. I’m proud to see Constellation Brands doubling down on Montana agriculture,” said Montana Senator Tim Sheehy (R-MT). “North Dakota is a leading producer of barley, with our farmers producing more than 28 million bushels last year. We appreciate this $100 million, five-year investment in North Dakota and the surrounding states’ barley industries. Our barley production is integral to the U.S. brewing industry and this investment will benefit both of these important industries,” said North Dakota Senator John Hoeven ( R-ND) , Chairman of the Senate Agriculture Appropriations Committee. “North Dakota is a leader in American barley and corn production, and today’s announcement from Constellation Brands is a long-term investment in the farmers who make that success possible. Our grain growers strengthen our national agricultural economy and supply chains, and they deserve the support to keep their farms resilient and sustainable,” said North Dakota Senator Kevin Cramer (R-ND). “Montana's farmers are the best in the world, and they deserve strong partners who are willing to invest in their future. I appreciate Constellation Brands’ continued commitment to Montana barley growers. Investments like this strengthen our agricultural economy and create more certainty for the producers who keep it moving,” said Montana Congressman Troy Downing (R-MT). “Thank you to Constellation for their recognition of and investment in Montana agriculture. Montana farmers grow some of the best products available. This expansion will build on the already strong ag economy and further strengthen our ag security. Bravo Zulu to all,” said Montana Congressman Ryan Zinke (R-MT). “I’m thrilled to see the $100 million investment supporting American barley farmers and strengthening the supply chain. As the nation’s leading barley-producing state, Idaho growers are powering our economy. I’m excited to celebrate this great news with barley growers nationwide,” said Idaho Congressman Mike Simpson (R-ID). “I’m thrilled to see Constellation Brands expanding its commitment to American agriculture through increased support for barley, hops, and corn farmers across Idaho, Montana, and North Dakota. Idaho is a leading producer of these vital crops, and this initiative will further strengthen our agricultural sector, give growers a greater voice, and support farming communities across our state,” said Idaho Congressman Russ Fulcher (R-ID). “This announcement helps deliver exactly what our farmers are asking for: more local markets. North Dakota’s barley, corn, and hops growers are proud to produce a quality product that is used and enjoyed right here in our own country. This is very welcome news from Constellation Brands right as producers are harvesting their fields. Thank you,” said North Dakota Congresswoman Julie Fedorchak (R-ND). “Constellation Brands current and future support for our agricultural community comes at a critical time.
