title: Email Clients With a Slack or iMessage AI Agent in 2026
summary: Handle your inbox from Slack or iMessage with a real slack email agent. Compare Slashy, Superhuman, and Shortwave to find the best AI assistant for 2026.
body_text: Founders in 2026 don't live in their inboxes. They live in Slack channels, Telegram groups, and iMessage threads where deals actually happen. Most email apps assume you want to spend your day staring at a list of threads. This creates a constant app-switching tax. You get a Slack notification about a deal, then you have to jump into your email to find the relevant thread, then jump back to Slack to update your team. The industry is moving toward the agentic inbox. This is not an email app with an AI button bolted on. It is a system where the email client works as a worker that follows you to where you already are. The useful test is whether you can approve a draft from your phone or trigger a follow-up from a chat thread without opening the email app at all. Which Email Clients Actually Have a Slack or iMessage Agent (Quick Answer) The market for AI email is crowded, but the number of tools with a functional Slack email agent is small. Most companies claim to have a Slack integration when they really just have a notification bot. A notification bot tells you that you have mail. An agent actually does the work for you. Slashy is a platform that offers a native iMessage/SMS agent (Slashy, 2026). This allows users to triage their inbox, approve drafts, and check their calendar through a chat interface. It is built for founders who are frequently away from their desks but need to keep momentum on sales and investor updates. Superhuman offers Slack integration, but it is focused on providing context for drafting emails within the Superhuman app. It does not give you a surface to act on mail from within iMessage. Shortwave supports a Slack integration and uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect with AI chat interfaces like Claude, but it lacks a dedicated mobile chat agent. Spark Mail uses Slack for team collaboration and sharing links to threads, but it does not offer a chatbot that can draft or send emails on your behalf. If your goal is to act on mail from inside your messaging apps rather than just be notified there, that is the specific capability to check for, and it is worth testing on your own inbox before you commit. What Separates a Real Agent From a Notification or Share Button Most software companies use the word agent to describe anything that uses a LLM. A share button is a shortcut. A notification is an interruption. A real Slack email agent is an autonomous loop. It should be able to take a high-level command and execute it across multiple steps. If you see a button that says "Share to Slack," you are looking at a legacy feature. That button requires you to be in the email app first. A real agent meets you in Slack when you are already there. A real agent has three specific traits. First, it is asynchronous. You can assign it a task (like "find the last proposal I sent to George") and it goes and does it while you stay in your conversation. Second, it has state. It knows what you were talking about five minutes ago. Third, it has write access. It can draft a reply in your voice and wait for your approval before sending. That is what an AI email agent actually does . Many tools fail because they only offer one-way communication. They push data from the inbox to Slack, but they cannot pull instructions from Slack back into the inbox. This forces you to switch apps anyway. In 2026, the standard for a Slack email agent is a two-way bridge. You should be able to see an urgent email in your Slack feed and type /draft-reply followed by your thoughts. The agent then creates the draft using your specific tone and recipient context. Anything less is a glorified notification system that adds to your cognitive load rather than reducing it. Slashy: iMessage Agent Built Into the Email Client Slashy is an AI-native intelligent inbox that treats its iMessage interface as a first-class citizen. It is built on top of Gmail and uses a proprietary memory system to learn your writing style over time (Slashy, 2026). Slashy provides a full iMessage and SMS interface. You can text your inbox. You can ask Slashy to draft a reply to an investor while you are walking between meetings, and it will use your previous conversations to get the tone right. It is aimed at founders and operators who manage high volumes of mail. It includes a Gmail MCP integration that lets you connect your email to other AI tools. The core value is handling busywork before you even open the app. Slashy drafts replies in your voice and labels incoming mail automatically. If a thread needs a follow-up, Slashy sends a reminder so deals do not go cold. On the data question: Slashy does not train AI models on your data, and enforces zero retention with its AI providers. It holds SOC 2 Type II and CASA Tier 2, encrypts data with AES-256 at rest and TLS 1.2+ in transit, and connects through Gmail OAuth that you can revoke from your Google account at any time. Full detail is on the security page, and pricing is public. Superhuman: Slack Context for Drafting, No iMessage Surface Superhuman is known for its speed and keyboard shortcuts, and its Slack integration is built to provide context rather than to act on your behalf. It can notify you when someone opens an email or when a specific VIP contacts you. These notifications are fast, but they are not agents. You still have to click the notification and open the Superhuman app to do anything meaningful. In 2026, Superhuman remains a desktop-first experience for people who enjoy the flow of a high-speed interface. It lacks a native iMessage agent that can draft or send mail via text. This makes it less suited for the founder who is constantly moving. It uses AI to summarize threads and help you write faster, and it is a strong choice if your working day happens at a desk. If what you want is something that acts on mail while you are away from your computer, that is a different shape of tool. Related reading: connecting an AI agent to Gmail with MCP . Shortwave: Slack Integration and MCP Tasklets, No iMessage Agent Shortwave focuses on a search-first approach to email. It has done solid work integrating with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows users to treat their email like a database that can be queried by AI assistants. Shortwave has a Slack integration that can push summaries of threads into your channels, which is useful for keeping a team informed. It also supports tasklets, which are small AI-driven actions you can trigger from the sidebar. The limitation is the lack of a mobile chat agent. While you can use Shortwave with Claude through an MCP server, there is no native way to text your inbox or manage your calendar via iMessage. Shortwave is excellent for researchers and deep-work enthusiasts who want to search their history with natural language. It is less suited to someone who wants to act on mail from a chat window. For users who want to build custom workflows via MCP, Shortwave is a strong contender, though it takes more setup than a chat agent you can use out of the box. Spark Mail: Slack Sharing for Teams, No Chat Agent Spark Mail has long been a favorite for teams because of its shared inbox features. It allows multiple people to view and comment on the same email thread. Its Slack integration is built around this collaboration. You can share a link to a Spark thread directly into a Slack channel, and your team can discuss it there. This is a useful feature for support teams or small groups of operators who need to coordinate on a response. Spark is not a Slack email agent. It does not have a chatbot you can talk to. It does not have an AI that drafts replies in your voice before you open the thread. Spark has added AI features for summarizing and editing text, and those are tools you use once you are already inside the email. It does not publish an iMessage or SMS surface for acting on mail. If you need to discuss emails with a team, Spark is excellent. If you need to get work done from a mobile chat window, it will fall short. How to Choose Based on Where You Actually Work Choosing the right email client in 2026 depends on where your attention lives. If you spend eight hours a day at a desk with a mechanical keyboard, a tool like Superhuman or Shortwave is a solid choice. They prioritize the desktop experience and provide the shortcuts you need to move through mail quickly. They are built for the era of the inbox as a destination. If you are a founder or a growth lead who spends most of your time in meetings, on calls, or in Slack, you need a Slack email agent. You cannot afford to open a separate app every time a notification pops up. You need a tool that lets you act. Of the tools here, Slashy is the one that publishes an iMessage and SMS surface, so you can check your calendar, draft replies, and triage mail without leaving your chat app. It turns your inbox into a background process rather than a foreground distraction. Evaluate these tools based on their mobile agent capabilities. Ask whether the tool can actually send an email from a text message. If it can only send you a link to click, it is not an agent. Use Slashy if you want an assistant that follows you to iMessage so you can focus on building your company instead of managing your folders. Conclusion The shift from inbox to agent is the biggest change in email since the smartphone. The useful one is whichever removes the need to open the email app at all. Slashy does that through an iMessage agent that drafts in your voice, tracks follow-ups, and reaches your calendar. It is designed for founders and operators who need to stay responsive without being tethered to a desk. If you are tired of constant app-switching between Slack and your inbox, visit Slashy and connect your Gmail to start managing your inbox through the chat apps you already use.

title: How to Make Your RFP Cover Letter Stand Out
summary: Craft a standout RFP cover letter with key tips on personalization, impactful greetings, and showcasing benefits. Make your proposal unforgettable!
body_text: Are you confident your RFP cover letter captures attention from the very first line? It should, because an RFP can play a significant role in shaping business opportunities. With so much effort and potential at stake, your cover letter is more than a polite introduction; it’s a strategic tool that sets the tone for your entire proposal. The Association of Proposal Management Professionals (APMP) notes that evaluators often skim the first page to quickly gauge whether a vendor understands their needs and can deliver results. Strong proposals highlight measurable outcomes, such as “Accelerated schedule delivered 30 days sooner than required” or “reduced order-handling costs by 30%.” This makes your cover letter prime real estate for creating a powerful first impression, showcasing your unique value, and setting the stage for the rest of your proposal. Before sending off your RFP response, take a moment to ensure your cover letter truly reflects the quality and intent of your submission. With a few focused tips and a quick review, you can ensure it conveys the right message from the very start. In this post, we’ll cover what a proposal cover letter is, why it matters, and how to craft one that positions you ahead of the competition. What This Blog Covers: Definition of an RFP cover letter and why it matters. Key components for a high-impact cover letter. Step-by-step process for writing one effectively. Difference between an RFP cover letter and an executive summary. Common mistakes to avoid and how to fix them. A ready-to-use template for quick customization. A final checklist to ensure quality before sending. How Inventive AI helps create faster, more tailored RFP responses. What Is an RFP Cover Letter? An RFP cover letter is a short, professional introduction that accompanies your full proposal when responding to a Request for Proposal (RFP). Unlike the detailed proposal that dives into your technical approach, pricing, and timelines, the cover letter serves as a high-level snapshot of your intent and capability. From a vendor’s perspective, it should: Introduce your company and the team behind the proposal. Acknowledge the buyer’s needs and show you understand their priorities. Highlight your key strengths and differentiators without overwhelming detail. Express enthusiasm for the opportunity to work together. Guide the reader to the proposal for more in-depth information. Think of it as the handshake before the conversation; it sets the tone and builds trust before they review the details. Why a Well-Written RFP Cover Letter Is Important A strong cover letter does more than check a box; it can determine whether your proposal gets noticed or ignored. With procurement teams juggling dozens of submissions and the RFP software market projected to surge from USD 2,275.93 million in 2024 to over USD 7,383.30 million by 2031 at a 15.83% CAGR ( Cognitive Market Research ), standing out is essential Here’s why it matters: First Impressions Count: Evaluators often skim the first page before diving deeper. A clear, engaging cover letter creates a positive initial perception. Shows You Understand the Client: Tailoring the letter to address their specific needs signals that you’ve done your homework and care about their goals. Positions Your Value Early: Highlighting your unique selling points up front helps evaluators remember you, even when comparing multiple vendors. Sets the Tone for the Proposal: The language, professionalism, and clarity in your cover letter can prime the reader for the quality of your full response. Saves Time for Busy Reviewers: A concise overview makes it easier for decision-makers to grasp your fit without sifting through the entire document right away. Basics of an RFP Cover Letter Before you start writing, it’s important to understand what an RFP cover letter should contain and how each part plays a role in capturing the evaluator’s attention. While the cover letter is typically no more than one page, every sentence should work toward building trust and interest. What Components Should Be Included? 1. Header and Contact Information Include your company name, address, contact details, and date. Add the recipient’s name, title, organization, and address. This ensures professionalism and clarity from the start. 2. Opening Greeting Address the recipient by name if possible (“Dear Ms. Johnson”) instead of generic greetings. A personalized salutation signals that the letter is tailored to them, not a copy-paste. Introduction Paragraph Briefly state your intent to submit the proposal and acknowledge the specific RFP name or number. Express appreciation for the opportunity. Example: “Thank you for the opportunity to respond to RFP #2026-01 for cloud migration services.” 3. Summarizing the RFP requirements This is where you briefly highlight your understanding of the client’s needs and summarize how you’ll solve their problem. Focus on outcomes, not just features. Keep it concise but impactful, this is often the part evaluators remember most. 4. Key Differentiators and Value Proposition Highlight what sets you apart (specialized expertise, proven results, certifications, innovative approach, etc.). Keep it to 2–3 bullet points for easy reading. 5. Closing Statement and Call to Action Reiterate your enthusiasm for the project. Invite them to reach out for clarifications or next steps. Example: “We look forward to the opportunity to partner with you and bring this project to life.” 6. Signature Block Include your name, title, and contact information. A handwritten or scanned signature can add a personal touch. The executive summary plays an important role in any RFP, but the cover letter, which appears right before it, often confuses. Many people mistake the two, so let’s break down what an executive summary is and why it’s different from the cover letter, even though both are essential parts of an RFP. What Is an Executive Summary? An executive summary is a concise overview of your entire proposal. It highlights: The client’s main challenges Your proposed solution The value and benefits you offer A brief outline of deliverables and outcomes Its goal is to let decision-makers quickly understand why your proposal is worth considering, without reading the full document first. Aspect RFP Cover Letter Executive Summary Purpose Build rapport, set the tone, and create interest in your proposal. Summarize the proposal’s key points and value. Tone Personal, conversational, and client-focused. Professional, concise, and fact-driven. Content Highlights your enthusiasm, credibility, and fit for the project. Covers problems, solutions, benefits, and results. Length Usually 1 page or less. 1–2 pages depending on proposal size. ‍ Avoid proposal inconsistencies and conflicts using our intelligent error detection and correction tools.. Book a free demo today! Whether you use your RFP cover letter as a quick introduction or a detailed pitch, remember, a real person is reading it. The quality of what you write often decides if they read every word, skim through in seconds, or skip it altogether. Most proposal cover letters stick in the reader’s mind for one reason or another: they’re either painfully bad or impressively good. Make sure yours falls into the second category. Step-by-Step: How to Write an Effective RFP Cover Letter An effective RFP cover letter is structured to instantly capture attention, build trust, and position you as the best choice. Here’s a step-by-step approach: 1) Address It to the Right People If you don’t already know who will review your proposal, find out. Contact the RFP coordinator to learn the names of the key decision-makers, this could be procurement staff, stakeholders, or executives. Avoid generic greetings like “To whom it may concern.” They signal that you didn’t take the time to personalize your letter. Addressing reviewers directly increases the likelihood they’ll read your letter and shows you’re invested in the relationship, not just the transaction. Evaluators spend about 2.5 hours per RFP , often taking two weeks for review. Inventive AI’s RFP software speeds up response creation with AI-tailored content, enabling faster, more accurate submissions. 2) Start With a Fresh, Human Opening Buyers read dozens of RFP responses, many of which sound alike. Don’t start with tired lines like “Thank you for the opportunity to earn your business.” Instead, open with a specific and sincere compliment, or acknowledge a business goal mentioned in their RFP. This quickly proves you’ve done your homework and sets you apart from copy-paste responses. Remember: The cover letter is your chance to connect on a human level before they get into the technical details. 3) Use Smart Formatting to Keep It Readable Your cover letter should be one page, cleanly formatted, and easy to scan. Break it into three strategic parts: Opening: Address by name + impactful first sentence. Middle: Use bullet points to spotlight your top strengths without directly comparing yourself to competitors. Examples: 99% on-time delivery Scalable solutions for multi-region rollout 24/7 client support with dedicated account managers Proven track record of increasing client efficiency by 20%+ Closing: End with a clear next step, such as scheduling a demo, requesting standard T&Cs, or arranging a reference call. By drawing attention to your differentiators, you help the reviewer focus on your value, even if they’re skimming. Leverage AI-powered, brand-aligned templates to craft polished proposals in a fraction of the time. Book a free demo today! 4) Show You Understand Their Needs Every RFP exists to solve a problem. Prove you know what that problem is. Mirror the language used in the RFP to summarize their challenge. Connect your expertise directly to their desired outcomes. Demonstrate that you’re thinking beyond the immediate project, you’re aiming for a long-term, strategic partnership. Example: “We understand your goal is to streamline vendor management while maintaining compliance across multiple regions. Our centralized dashboard and SLA tracking tools are built for exactly this challenge.” 5) Add a Brief, Relevant Success Story Evidence builds credibility. Include a short example of how you’ve solved a similar problem. Keep it to 2–3 sentences: Client → Challenge → Solution → Result . Use metrics or timeframes to strengthen impact. Example: “For ACME Corp, we implemented a regional rollout in under 8 weeks, cutting processing time by 35% and boosting end-user satisfaction to 92%.” 6) Stay True to Your Brand Voice An RFP process may be formal, but your cover letter should still reflect your company’s personality and values. If your culture is approachable and collaborative, let that tone come through. Use “we” statements that frame shared goals: “We believe our platform will free your team to focus on strategic initiatives while we handle day-to-day automation.” Consistency between your cover letter, executive summary, and proposal helps build trust. 7) Close With a Strong Call to Action, Contact Info, and Signature The end of your letter should tell the reader exactly what to do next. Be specific: “Let’s schedule a 30-minute session to walk through our solution in detail” or “Please share your standard T&Cs so we can move forward.” Include your direct contact information. Sign the letter, digitally or by hand, to add a personal touch. Choosing the signer: In most cases, it’s best for the account owner to sign, as they have the client relationship. For high-value RFPs, a VP or CEO signature can convey commitment and authority. Example of a Strong RFP Cover Letter (Template) Here’s a professional, ready-to-use structure you can adapt for any RFP. Simply replace the placeholders with your project-specific details. [Your Name] [Your Job Title] [Your Company Name] [Company Address] [City, State, ZIP] [Email Address] | [Phone Number] [Date] [Recipient Name] [Recipient Job Title] [Client/Organization Name] [Client Address] [City, State, ZIP] Dear [Recipient Name or “Evaluation Committee”], Opening Paragraph: We are pleased to submit our proposal in response to [RFP Title / RFP Number] for [Project Name]. After reviewing your requirements, we understand your goals are to [briefly mention top 2–3 client priorities or challenges]. With our proven expertise in [relevant service or industry], we are confident we can deliver exceptional results that align with your vision. Middle Section – Key Strengths: Our team brings a unique combination of experience, innovation, and commitment. Highlights include: [Key Strength #1] – How it benefits the client. title: Runware Is Putting AI Inference Into Portable Pods
summary: Runware's portable Sonic Inference Pods promise dense, water-free AI capacity that can be deployed near users in weeks instead of years.
body_text: Runware via TechCrunch · Source image AI News Runware Is Putting AI Inference Into Portable Pods Runware's portable Sonic Inference Pods promise dense, water‑free AI capacity that can be deployed near users in weeks instead of years. The giant AI campus has a smaller challenger: a shipping‑container‑sized inference system that can be placed where power and demand already exist. Runware has launched its Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center designed to add serving capacity without waiting years for a conventional facility. 1 while. 2 What is inside the pod Runware describes Sonic as a vertically integrated system: custom boards, Nvidia GPUs, servers, storage, networking, cooling and inference software are designed as one stack. The company claims this yields twice the inference throughput for leading open‑source models and materially lower capital and operating costs. 1 not independent benchmark results. The hardware is intended for model serving rather than frontier‑scale training. That focus matters because inference workloads are numerous, geographically distributed and sensitive to latency. A training cluster can live far from users; an interactive image, video or voice product benefits when capacity is nearby. Speed comes from construction, not only chips Runware says a pod can be deployed in roughly three weeks rather than the multi‑year timetable of a large data center. 2 Modular capacity lets an operator build in increments instead of forecasting an entire campus years in advance. That changes the financial risk. A company can add a pod when utilization justifies it, move closer to a customer cluster and avoid some stranded‑capacity exposure. It does not eliminate permitting, electricity or network requirements; it packages them into a smaller and potentially faster project. Closed‑loop cooling is the timely advantage The pod uses closed‑loop cooling and does not consume water during normal operation, according to Runware. The timing is notable because communities are scrutinizing AI facilities for water use and power costs. On the same news cycle, Texas ordered comprehensive audits of proposed data centers before allowing them to connect to the grid. Portable hardware is not automatically sustainable. A one‑megawatt load remains substantial, and the emissions depend on the electricity source. The credible benefit is narrower: a sealed cooling loop can reduce local water pressure, and deployment near available generation may reduce the need for some new transmission. A distributed network can improve resilience Runware says requests can move among pods based on location and available capacity. If one unit fails, traffic can be routed elsewhere rather than treating a whole site as a single failure domain. Customers can also reserve full pods for dedicated hardware. 2 The operational challenge is coordination. Distributed systems create more sites to secure, monitor and maintain. Consistent model versions, data handling, incident response and network performance must be proven across every location. Modularity moves complexity; it does not make complexity disappear. Developers may get a new infrastructure option For AI application teams, the relevant question is not whether a pod looks novel. It is whether the provider can deliver predictable latency, availability, price and model coverage. Runware says its system can host any model and provides a large model lake with fast cold starts. 1 If the economics hold under real customer loads, modular inference could sit between hyperscale cloud APIs and self‑hosted GPU clusters. That would be useful for media generation, regional data requirements and workloads with steady utilization but no appetite for operating physical infrastructure. The proof still needs independent numbers Runware's throughput, cost and deployment comparisons are supplied by Runware. The company has not published audited total‑cost assumptions, failure rates or standardized third‑party benchmarks for the new pods. Ten deployments demonstrate activity, not yet a global operating record. The launch is still consequential because it makes a concrete bet about where AI infrastructure goes next: away from a few enormous campuses and toward smaller serving nodes close to demand. The next evidence should be customer latency, sustained utilization, energy intensity and the cost of maintaining a fleet. Sources 1. Runware says a 20-foot pod can hold one megawatt of high-density compute (runware.ai) 2. title: Designing Anti-Fraud UX: Protecting Users from Digital Scams
summary: Understand the importance of Anti-Fraud UX in addressing online fraud and safeguarding users from scams.
body_text: Traditional security infrastructure prioritizes system-level defenses — securing databases, locking down cloud servers and configuring firewalls. Modern scams bypass code by exploiting a different vulnerability: human behavior. By going after users directly, scams have become more pervasive. Data from a Stop Scams Alliance and Gallup report shows that online fraud affects 24% of Americans and costs roughly $68 billion every year. That’s over four times higher than official federal tracking systems show in 2025, according to the same report. Beyond lost revenue, fraud inflicts severe emotional distress on its victims. “ Fear of being tricked again destroys customer trust. Many users stop buying things online entirely which impacts platform sales,” according to Surekha Nagpal, Senior Director, FinCrimes & Risk Operations, TaskUs. Backend security is insufficient. Companies need to build protections into the brand experience and educate consumers on financial crime prevention . What security information should merchants share To stop fraud, platforms need to clear up the confusion that scammers rely on. Bad actors succeed by perfectly imitating trusted brands, but clearly defining how a business operates makes it harder for them to deceive users. Product and trust teams can protect customers by focusing on three main areas. 1. Communication channels and off-platform links Data from the Stop Scams Alliance and Gallup report lists where most scams start: online shopping platforms (17%), phone calls (15%), social media posts (12%) and text messages (10%). “Scammers often start a conversation on your platform and try to move the user to a different app quickly to avoid safety filters,” Surekha explains. According to the report, 50% of successful scams use two or more communication methods to trap a user. To protect customers, platforms should explicitly share a list of all official websites, emails, phone numbers and social media handles. At the same time, remind users that requests to move interactions from your secure native messaging environment to external apps (such as WhatsApp, Discord or Telegram) is a strong indicator of a scam. 2. Passwords and false urgency The same study notes that 44% of victims voluntarily give up their passwords or personal details during an attack. This single mistake causes financial losses to jump, raising the median loss from $350 to $500 per incident. Surekha recommends that platforms constantly reinforce a strict “never ask” rule to prevent this. Remind customers that staff will never ask for a password, login code or full credit card number. Teach them how to spot high-pressure tactics. Scammers often create fake emergencies by claiming an account will be closed immediately. Amplify the message that official customer service teams will never use threats to verify identity. 3. Restricted payment methods Scammers prefer fast, permanent payment methods because the money cannot be recovered. Payment apps or services are used in 42% of scams, followed by credit or debit cards at 31%, according to Stop Scams Alliance-Gallup. In the majority of cases, the victim never gets any of their money back. Surekha says that to counter the threat, instruct users to complete transactions strictly inside the built-in checkout system. Clear warnings should state that if a seller asks for payment through outside peer-to-peer apps, gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency, they are breaking safety rules and automatically lose their customer protection. Designing UX safety features for every stage of the user journey While sharing this information is vital, dumping long pages of warnings on users during checkout hurts sales. Instead, fraud prevention strategies include “just-in-time” user experience (UX) — micro-interactions and dynamic safety alerts — based on specific customer actions. 1. In-app security alerts People rarely read help articles and terms of service hidden in a website’s footer. It’s better to use quick alerts. For example, placing a small note next to a payment form that says, “Keep your money safe. Never pay outside this app,” catches the user right before they make a decision. Companies working with multiple vendors can use badges to indicate that a seller has completed strict Know Your Business (KYB) checks. 2. Post-purchase safety Scammers often use phishing texts after a real purchase, claiming users need to pay a shipping fee or fix an address. Platforms can stop this by clarifying their shipping process in the order confirmation email: “We only ship via [Carrier Name] and will never text you to ask for extra fees.” 3. Easy reporting portal Most fraud goes unreported because users feel it won’t help or they don’t know where to turn. Platforms can bridge this gap by adding a simple, one-click “Report Suspicious Behavior” button directly on order history and profile pages. Best practices for mapping retail platform safety features Lifecycle stage User activity Core function What to do Discovery Account setup Identity verification Deploy compliance tools like 3DS2, device tracking and MFA to block fake accounts Transaction Checkout In-App security notices Show real-time alerts (e.g., “Never pay outside this app” ) right on the payment screen Fulfillment Order review Post-purchase safety info Show clear examples of what official delivery tracking messages look like Support Reporting fraud One-click reporting Provide a visible “Report Suspicious Behavior” option Building long-term platform trust “Digital security is a core part of the customer experience,” says Surekha, ”Proactively guiding users protects both user funds and platform reputation.” By delivering clear, actionable consumer guidance alongside integrated product safety deliverables, modern merchants can establish resilient, high-integrity marketplaces built to withstand digital fraud.
